title: Game Programming with raylib
tagline: Make real 2D and 3D games in C++ with a small, friendly library
description: raylib opens a window, draws shapes, sprites, text and 3D models, plays sounds and reads input, all from a few plain C functions. The course builds a series of small complete games and the game-programming ideas behind them: the game loop, frame time, sprites and animation, collision and platformer physics, cameras, tile maps, enemies and pathfinding, a first 3D scene, shaders, saving and packaging. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course. You build the games in Visual Studio; the practice on the site checks the game logic inside them.

milestones.title: The Game Loop
milestones.blurb: Setting raylib up, the loop every game runs, coordinates, shapes and colours, frame time, and reading the keyboard, mouse and gamepad.

lessons.title: What raylib Is and Setting It Up
lessons.summary: raylib is a small C library for making games - windows, drawing, input, sound and 3D in a few hundred plain functions. This lesson explains what it does and does not do, installs it with vcpkg, and runs a first window in Visual Studio.

lessons.title: The Game Loop
lessons.summary: Every game is a loop that reads input, updates the world and draws it, many times a second. This lesson takes raylib's loop apart - what BeginDrawing and EndDrawing do, why the screen is cleared every frame, and how to keep update and drawing apart.

lessons.title: Coordinates, Shapes and Colours
lessons.summary: Where things go on the screen and how to draw them - raylib's coordinate system with y pointing down, Vector2 and Rectangle, the shape functions, colours with alpha, and centring things on the screen.

lessons.title: Frame Time and Smooth Movement
lessons.summary: Moving "4 pixels a frame" runs twice as fast on a 120 Hz screen. This lesson moves things in units per second using the frame time, adds velocity and acceleration, normalises diagonal movement, and keeps big frame-time spikes from breaking the game.

lessons.title: Keyboard, Mouse and Gamepad Input
lessons.summary: Reading every kind of input raylib supports - keys held and pressed, typed characters, the mouse and its wheel, and gamepads with their sticks and dead zones - and mapping them to game actions so players can rebind them.

milestones.title: Sprites, Sound and Screens
milestones.blurb: Textures and sprite sheets, animation, text and a simple interface, sound effects and music, and organising a game into screens.

lessons.title: Textures and Sprites
lessons.summary: Loading images onto the GPU as textures, drawing them whole or in part, scaling, rotating and tinting them with DrawTexturePro, the origin point, flipping, and loading and unloading assets at the right time.

lessons.title: Sprite Sheets and Animation
lessons.summary: Animation is a sequence of frames shown one after another. This lesson cuts frames out of a sprite sheet, plays them at their own speed using a timer, handles looping and one-shot animations, and switches between animations as a character's state changes.

lessons.title: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
lessons.summary: Drawing text with raylib's default font and with your own fonts, measuring and aligning it, formatting numbers with TextFormat, and building the interface a small game needs - a score display, health bar, buttons and a menu you can use with keys or the mouse.

lessons.title: Sound and Music
lessons.summary: Playing sound effects and streaming music with raylib's audio module - the audio device, Sound versus Music, volume and pitch, playing the same sound many times at once, a little random variation, and volume settings in decibels and percentages.

lessons.title: Screens and Game States
lessons.summary: A finished game has a title screen, the game itself, a pause menu, a game-over screen and transitions between them. This lesson organises a game into screens - first with an enum and a switch, then with screen objects on a stack - and fades smoothly from one to the next.

milestones.title: Collision and Physics
milestones.blurb: Detecting and resolving collisions, gravity and jumping that feel good, fixed time steps, and spatial grids for many objects.

lessons.title: Detecting Collisions
lessons.summary: The collision tests 2D games are built on - point in rectangle, rectangle against rectangle, circle against circle and circle against rectangle - how each one works, raylib's functions for them, and choosing the right shape for each object.

lessons.title: Resolving Collisions
lessons.summary: Knowing two things overlap is half the job; the other half is deciding what happens. This lesson pushes objects apart along the shortest way out, moves one axis at a time so characters slide along walls, and stops fast objects from tunnelling through thin walls.

lessons.title: Gravity, Jumping and Game Feel
lessons.summary: Jumping that feels good is designed, not simulated. This lesson derives gravity and jump speed from the height and time you want, then adds the tricks platformers rely on - variable jump height, faster falling, coyote time, jump buffering and acceleration on the ground and in the air.

lessons.title: Fixed Time Steps
lessons.summary: Physics that depends on the frame time behaves slightly differently at every frame rate. A fixed time step runs the simulation in equal steps whatever the frame rate - this lesson builds the accumulator loop, guards against the spiral of death, and interpolates between steps for smooth drawing.

lessons.title: Spatial Grids for Many Objects
lessons.summary: Testing every object against every other is n squared - fine for 50 objects, hopeless for 5000. A uniform grid puts each object in the cells it touches and only tests objects that share a cell. This lesson builds one, rebuilds it every frame, and avoids testing pairs twice.

milestones.title: Worlds
milestones.blurb: Cameras and scrolling, tile maps and levels, particles and effects, enemies with state machines, and pathfinding on a grid.

lessons.title: Cameras and Scrolling Worlds
lessons.summary: A world bigger than the screen needs a camera. This lesson uses raylib's Camera2D - target, offset, zoom and rotation - converts between screen and world coordinates, and makes the camera follow the player smoothly with a dead zone, look-ahead, limits at the level's edges and screen shake.

lessons.title: Tile Maps and Levels
lessons.summary: Most 2D levels are grids of tiles. This lesson stores a tile map, draws only the visible part from a tile sheet, loads levels from text files, places objects such as the player's start and enemies from the same file, and picks wall tiles automatically from their neighbours.

lessons.title: Particles and Effects
lessons.summary: Dust, sparks, smoke and explosions are particles - many small, short-lived objects. This lesson builds a particle system with a fixed pool, emitters with randomised properties, values that change over a particle's life, and additive blending, plus the small effects that make a game feel alive.

lessons.title: Enemies and State Machines
lessons.summary: Enemies that patrol, notice the player, chase, attack and give up feel smart, but are a handful of states and the rules for moving between them. This lesson builds enemy behaviour as a finite state machine with enter and exit actions, timers, line of sight, and a little randomness.

lessons.title: Pathfinding on a Grid
lessons.summary: Walking straight at the player gets enemies stuck on walls. This lesson finds paths around obstacles on a tile map - breadth-first search for equal costs, A* with a heuristic for speed, costs for different terrain, and flow fields when many enemies chase one target.

milestones.title: 3D and Shaders
milestones.blurb: A first 3D scene, first-person movement, picking and 3D collision, shaders, and post-processing with render textures.

lessons.title: A First 3D Scene
lessons.summary: raylib draws 3D as easily as 2D. This lesson sets up a Camera3D, explains 3D coordinates and perspective, draws cubes, spheres, planes and a grid, loads and draws models, and introduces the vectors and matrices that move things in 3D.

lessons.title: Moving in 3D
lessons.summary: Walking around a 3D world - raylib's built-in camera modes, then a first-person controller of your own with yaw and pitch from the mouse, movement relative to where you look, gravity and jumping, and a third-person camera that orbits the player.

lessons.title: Picking and 3D Collision
lessons.summary: Clicking on things in 3D, shooting, line of sight and camera collision all ask one question - what does this ray hit first? This lesson turns the mouse into a ray, tests rays against planes, spheres and boxes, and adds sphere and box collision for moving objects.

lessons.title: Shaders
lessons.summary: Shaders are small programs that run on the GPU for every vertex and every pixel. This lesson explains vertex and fragment shaders, writes GLSL fragment shaders for raylib, passes values in with uniforms, and builds a flash effect, a dissolve and a simple light.

lessons.title: Render Textures and Post-Processing
lessons.summary: Drawing into a texture instead of the screen opens up a lot - pixel-perfect scaling, minimaps, split screens, and post-processing effects applied to the whole frame such as vignettes, colour grading, blur and scanlines.

milestones.title: Finishing a Game
milestones.blurb: Saving progress and settings, packaging a game for Windows and the web, and planning and building a complete small game.

lessons.title: Saving Progress and Settings
lessons.summary: Players expect a game to remember their settings, their progress and their best scores. This lesson chooses what to save and where, writes simple versioned text formats, saves safely so a crash never destroys a save, and keeps a high-score table.

lessons.title: Packaging a Finished Game
lessons.summary: Turning a project that runs on your computer into a game anyone can download - release builds, loading assets reliably, an asset cache, the window and icon, testing on a clean machine, a web build with Emscripten, and publishing on itch.io.

lessons.title: Project: A Complete Small Game
lessons.summary: Put the whole course together into one finished game - choosing a scope you can finish, the order to build it in, data-driven waves and levels, the polish that makes it feel complete, and a checklist for release. The example is a top-down arena survival game.
